claims.text: High configurational entropy in HEAs promotes preferential surface segregation of reactive elements such as Cr, Al, or Si.
The segregated reactive elements rapidly oxidize to form a continuous, adherent protective oxide layer.
The continuous, adherent oxide layer enhances oxidation resistance.
Casting or homogenization can produce HEA samples with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Selective surface enrichment of reactive alloying elements provides nucleation sites for protective oxide formation.
High configurational entropy in HEAs enhances atomic diffusion.
Enhanced atomic diffusion leads to localized enrichment of reactive elements at the alloy surface.
Under oxidizing conditions, surface-enriched reactive elements rapidly form a coherent and adherent oxide layer.
The coherent and adherent oxide layer protects the underlying metal from further oxidation.
HEAs will form a more uniform, continuous, and adherent oxide scale than compositionally similar lower-entropy conventional alloys under identical oxidation conditions.
HEAs will exhibit lower oxidation-induced mass gain than the conventional-alloy baseline.

Conventional alloys with comparable reactive-element content but lower configurational entropy will form discontinuous or less protective oxide layers because their surface-segregation effects are limited.
The proposed mechanism is expected to operate only under high-temperature oxidation conditions, exemplified by temperatures above 800 °C.
The proposed mechanism requires a sufficient reactive-element fraction, typically greater than 15%.
Changes in alloy composition, lower temperatures, or different oxidizing environments may suppress the proposed behavior.
The exact kinetics and quantitative impact of configurational entropy on protective-oxide formation are unresolved.
The direct contribution of high configurational entropy to oxidation resistance is uncertain.
A controlled comparison should hold reactive-element content, pretreatment, temperature, atmosphere, and exposure duration comparable while varying configurational entropy.
The hypothesis is falsified if the HEAs show no statistically significant improvement in oxide continuity, oxidation mass gain, and oxide adhesion relative to the lower-entropy controls.
The hypothesis is also falsified if observed differences are fully attributable to reactive-element content rather than configurational entropy.
